Honors Contracts: FAQ for Faculty For the URI Honors Program Web Page (Draft Dec. 4, 2024) What is an Honors Contract? Honors contracts allow students to earn Honors credit for non-Honors courses by pursuing more advanced study. This requires an agreement between the student and instructor, and approval from the Honors Program. This option is valuable for students interested in a course not offered in an Honors format or whose schedules prevent them from enrolling in an Honors section. Why should we use Honors Contracts? Honors Contracts offer several beneﬁts: Flexibility: They allow students to tailor their education to their interests and goals. Accessibility: They provide opportunities for honors-level work when there are limitations on the number of honors courses offered. Student Engagement: They empower students, foster motivation, and facilitate mentor-mentee relationships with faculty. Who can supervise an Honors contract? All full-time faculty may supervise an Honors contract. No one, however, is required to do so. Part-time faculty and staff may supervise contracts only in special cases if an exception is granted prior to the creation of a contract by the Honors Program. What are the faculty roles and responsibilities in an Honors contract? Faculty roles and responsibilities include: Helping the student formulate a proposal for an appropriate contract project.

Deﬁning the terms and timeline of the contract with the student.
Providing guidance as the student works on the contracted project, with at least one mid-project meeting.
Evaluating the contract project at the end of the semester.
How much time should faculty plan to devote to this?
Generally, a faculty member should expect to devote 3-5 hours over the course of a term on a contracted project.
How are Honors Contracts set up?
The Honors Program provides comprehensive guidelines and support for setting up contracts on its Web site (See “The Contract Process”.
Students are encouraged to communicate early with instructors and the Honors Program to explore possibilities and ensure a clear understanding of the process.
Brieﬂy: The Honors contract process involves four stages: 1.
Crafting of an individualized project with the course instructor. 2.
Submission of the contract to the Honors Program for approval. 3.
Completion of the agreed-upon assignments and activities. 4.
Submission of the completed work and the Honors Contract Completion Form confirming the instructor’s satisfaction with the work.
What should be included in an Honors Contract?
The Honors contract proposal consists of three parts: 1.

The Contract Form, signed by both the student and the instructor. 2.
A copy of the original course syllabus 3.
A brief description of the proposed project (500-1000 words.) The following information should be included in the proposal: 1.
What?
Why?
When?
How? – A brief overview of the project, its rationale, timeline and evaluation criteria. 2.
How is it "honors"? – How, precisely the project differs from the regular work of the class.
I.e: A clear articulation of how the contract meets the "broader, deeper, more complex" criteria of the National Collegiate Honors Council. 3.
What will we see? – What will the outcome (or deliverable) of the project be?

4.
A timetable – E.g.: Meetings with the course instructor, a mid-term check-in, submission of components or drafts of the project, and the submission of the final product.
The final deadline can be no later than the scheduled final exam period for the course. 5.
Evaluation criteria – Include a clear statement of the criteria that will be used to evaluate the contracted work.
What are the minimum requirements that must be met in order to be judged acceptable?
If there are multiple elements, how do they each contribute?
Also, the following wording must be included in the proposal: "The Honors contract work will be assessed as Satisfactory or Unsatisfactory by the instructor according to the criteria described in this contract.
The rating will be entered into a Honors Contract Completion form.
A rating of Satisfactory will result in the student receiving Honors credit for the course.
A rating of Unsatisfactory will result in no Honors credit being awarded for the course.
Performance on the Honors Contract work will not affect the ﬁnal grade in any circumstance." The Honors Program may approve the proposal as written, request more information before making a decision, or reject it.

Once approved, the Honors Administrator will sign it and send a copy to both the student and the instructor.
Approved contracts result in a transcript notation of "Honors" for the course in question once Enrollment Services is notiﬁed by Honors that the coursework has been completed.
What are some examples of positive outcomes from Honors Contracts?
When well-managed, Honors Contracts can: • Cultivate personalized learning experiences. • Develop strong mentoring relationships between students and faculty. • Enhance the overall honors experience. • Provide faculty with a new vision for their courses.
What are some potential problems with Honors Contracts, and how can they be avoided?
Some potential issues include: Routine or Casual Use: Contracts should not become commonplace or be considered a replacement of the regular honors curriculum.

Lack of Meaningful Interaction: Although the contracted projects require only about 20 hours of work by the student and 3 to 5 hours of work by the faculty, it is important to ensure that contracts involve meaningful interaction between students and instructors. Unclear Expectations: The Honors Program provides clear guidelines and assessment criteria to students and faculty maintain high standards. Faculty are be expected to provide clear instructions to the students in the contract language. How can I ensure that Honors Contracts are effective? To ensure effectiveness: Maintain high standards and clear expectations. Ensure that the contracted work is well-connected to the course themes and outcomes. Ensure that the contracted work enhances the student’s experience of the course themes, materials, and outcomes. Will I be compensated for my work with Honors Contracts? Yes, it is essential that faculty are recognized and compensated for the additional work involved in Honors Contracts. Your work should be noted in your review portfolio. What is the difference between an Honors contract and an Honors Project? An Honors contract deﬁnes a project requiring approximately 20 hours of work, appended to an existing non-Honors course to allow the course’s credits be counted as Honors credits. An Honors project is a mentored independent study for 3 or 6 credits, devoted to a project that requires extensive research, reading, writing, creativity, or experimentation.

How is an Honors contract satisﬁed? An Honors contract is satisﬁed when the professor notiﬁes the Honors Program that the student has completed the assigned task satisfactorily. The student must also receive a B or higher in the course in order to earn Honors credit. Approved contract work should proceed according to the predetermined schedule. The project may, however, evolve as it progresses. Completed projects will not generally be expected to perfectly match the initial proposal. However, the student and instructor may along the way agree on signiﬁcant alterations, deviating substantially from the approved proposal. Should this occur, the student must submit an amended Honors contract proposal outlining the new criteria for completion and assessment. If in doubt on how to proceed contact the Honors Program as soon as possible. What happens if a student fails to complete an Honors contract? If a student fails to complete the proposed work to the satisfaction of the instructor, they will not receive Honors credit for the course. Can Honors contracts be applied to all courses? No, Honors contracts cannot be completed during the summer or J-Term. Nor should they be applied to 100-level courses, internships, independent studies, study abroad, or courses taken at other institutions.

Goal 1: Graduates will be prepared to enter research-focused graduate programs based on their knowledge of empirically- supported psychological processes and how to apply this knowledge to promote health and welfare.
Goal 2: Graduates will be competent in intermediate level critical thinking and behavioral data analysis skills.
Goal 3: Graduates will be able to work ethically in settings that emphasize diversity and global thinking.
The BS in Psychology is described to students as a program that focuses on the empirical and methodological aspects of psychology, that emphasizes math, science, and research methods in creating and applying psychological knowledge, and that includes a requirement in hands on research experience.
This program addresses Strategy 1 of the Agenda for Change (Infuse Anti-Racism, Social Justice and DEI Perspectives) in the Curriculum in several ways.
The introductory course (PSY 113) required of all majors, includes sections on anti-racism.
The lead instructor for this course has published multiple papers on teaching anti-racism and social justice.

Goal 3 of the BS program focuses on teaching students to work ethically in settings that emphasize diversity.

We wish now to make it a required course for all PSY BS majors.

Mark Robbins A BS in psychology prepares students for a wide variety of career options.
According to the website of the American Psychological Association ( https://www.apa.org/ed/precollege/psn/2018/01/bachelors-degree ), about 25 percent of psychology baccalaureates go to graduate school in psychology, about 18 percent go on for more education but not in psychology, and 57 percent are workforce graduates (Lin, Christidis & Stamm, 2017).
The BS degree prepares graduates especially well to apply to doctoral or other research-oriented advanced degrees in Psychology or other fields.

For those who do not wish to obtain an advanced degree, there are many job opportunities.
The above referenced website lists 70 job titles that students with a BS in Psychology are prepared for.
The BS degree with its focus on methodology, scientific writing, and statistical analysis especially trains graduates for any type of position requiring analytic, scientific writing, or data analytic skills, such as data base design analyst, research assistant, systems analyst, technical writer, information specialist, or data base manager.
A number of these occupations are considered high impact jobs in RI.
The Occupational Outlook Handbook of the Bureau of Labor ( https://www.bls.gov/ooh/field-of- degree/psychology/psychology-field-of-degree.htm ) indicates that the median salary for those with a degree in Psychology is $50,000 and that 60% are employed in occupations requiring at least a bachelor's degree.
Many department faculty offer students the opportunity to serve as undergraduate teaching assistants for course credit.
There are no paid undergraduate assistantships.
Graduate teaching assistantships are offered to assist instructors with PSY 200, PSY 301, and PSY 435.

Among peer institutions (UMass, UConn, UVM, UNH, U of Maine, and U of Delaware) BS degrees in Psychology are offered by three (UMASS, UCONN, and UVM).
The University of Delaware offers a BS in Neuroscience but not Psychology.
UNH and U of Maine offer only BA programs.
It does not make URI unique in our region to offer this degree, but if we did not offer it, we would not be keeping up with the more research/science oriented institutions in our region.
There is a trend among peer institutions to emphasize the scientific basis of psychology, which the proposed changes to the program are designed to accomplish.
